name: Rwanda
info: A small, densely peopled East African republic, independent from Belgium in 1962, whose Hutu-led governments ended in the 1994 genocide of the Tutsi, rebuilt since by the Rwandan Patriotic Front as an authoritarian, fast-growing state.

facts.founder: Grégoire Kayibanda, first president of the Hutu-dominated republic of 1962
facts.predecessor: The Kingdom of Rwanda under the Tutsi Nyiginya kings; German East Africa (1897–1916); the Belgian mandate and trust territory of Ruanda-Urundi (1916–1962)

t: Germany (1897) and Belgium (1916) ruled through the Tutsi king and treated Hutu and Tutsi as different races; Belgium's identity cards of 1935 fixed the labels, and the Hutu revolution of 1959 drove over 100,000 Tutsi into exile before independence on 1 July 1962.

Between 500,000 and 1,000,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu were killed in about 100 days from 6 April 1994 in attacks planned and ordered by the interim government; the RPF's military victory in July ended the genocide.

Under the RPF and Paul Kagame, president since 2000, poverty fell from 60.3% in 2000 to 27.4% in 2024 and the economy grew 9.4% in 2025, while elections are manipulated and Human Rights Watch documents detention, disappearances and torture.
dyk: Rwanda joined the Commonwealth of Nations in 2009 as one of its few members with no historical link to the British Empire, and in 2008 it changed the medium of instruction in its schools from French to English.
ev: The Rwandan Revolution: Hutu activists kill Tutsi and burn their houses, driving more than 100,000 people into neighbouring countries.
On 1 July Rwanda, separated from Burundi after a 1961 referendum abolished the monarchy, becomes independent under President Grégoire Kayibanda.
Juvénal Habyarimana takes power in a military coup; pro-Hutu discrimination continues with less violence and more prosperity.
The Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed of Tutsi refugees, invades northern Rwanda from Uganda, beginning the Rwandan Civil War.
On 6 April Habyarimana's plane is shot down near Kigali; within hours the genocide begins, killing 500,000 to 1,000,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about 100 days.
The RPF takes control of the whole country, ending the genocide; some two million Hutu flee to Zaïre and other neighbours.
Paul Kagame, the RPF's former commander, becomes president; a constitution follows in 2003 after a national referendum.
On 25 January the Democratic Republic of the Congo severs diplomatic relations over Rwanda's support for the M23 rebellion after the Goma offensive.

sections.foundation:
Rwanda's hills were settled by hunter-gatherers, ancestors of the Twa, then by farmers and herders and, between 800 BCE and 1500 CE, by Bantu groups who cleared forest for farming. Whether Hutu and Tutsi arrived as separate peoples or grew apart as classes within one society is disputed. From the 15th century the clans merged into kingdoms, one of which, under King Gihanga, absorbed its neighbours to form the Kingdom of Rwanda. Ruled by the Tutsi Nyiginya clan, it dominated from the mid-18th century and reached its greatest extent under Kigeli Rwabugiri in the 19th, whose ubuhake clientage and uburetwa corvée opened a rift between Hutu and Tutsi.

The Berlin Conference of 1884 assigned the territory to Germany, which allied with the king in 1897 and ruled through him and the existing hierarchy. Belgian forces invaded in 1916, and from 1922 Belgium governed Ruanda-Urundi as a League of Nations mandate and, like the Germans, promoting Tutsi supremacy as a matter of race; identity cards of 1935 labelled every person Tutsi, Hutu, Twa or Naturalised. Tension between Tutsi and the Hutu emancipation movement broke into the 1959 Rwandan Revolution, in which Hutu activists killed Tutsi, burned their houses and drove more than 100,000 into exile. The now pro-Hutu Belgians held a referendum in 1961 that abolished the monarchy, and on 1 July 1962 Rwanda, separated from Burundi, became independent under President Grégoire Kayibanda.
sections.socioeconomy:
Rwanda, the 'land of a thousand hills', is 26,338 square kilometres of highland a few degrees south of the Equator, one of the most densely peopled countries on earth, with about 14 million inhabitants. Nearly all are Banyarwanda, one people speaking Kinyarwanda, within which the Hutu were estimated at 84%, the Tutsi at 15% and the Twa at 1% in 2009. More than two thirds of households farm: matoke bananas cover over a third of the farmland, with potatoes, beans, sweet potatoes, cassava and maize; coffee and tea are the cash crops, more than 400,000 people living from coffee. Agriculture employs 64.5% of workers but yields 20% of output, services 52% and industry 22%.

The genocide wrecked the economy, and recovery has been the state's great project. GDP grew 8.2% in 2023, 8.9% in 2024 and 9.4% in 2025; poverty fell from 60.3% in 2000 to 27.4% in 2024, and life expectancy rose from 46.6 years in 2000 to 65.4 in 2021. Tourism is the leading earner of foreign exchange, over 1.4 million visitors in 2023 bringing about US$620 million, drawn above all by mountain gorillas in Volcanoes National Park at US$1,500 a permit. Yet Rwanda remained a least developed country in 2024, with GNI per head of US$3,620 and a third of children under five malnourished. Catholics (43.7% in 2012), Protestants (37.7%) and Adventists (11.8%) make up most of the population.
sections.military:
Independent Rwanda was born in violence. Exile raids and reprisals against Tutsi civilians followed 1962, and in 1973 Juvénal Habyarimana seized power in a coup. In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), a rebel force of Tutsi refugees, invaded from Uganda and began the Rwandan Civil War; by 1993 Habyarimana was forced into the Arusha Accords. The cease-fire ended on 6 April 1994 when his plane was shot down near Kigali Airport. Within hours the genocide began: over about 100 days between 500,000 and 1,000,000 Tutsi and politically moderate Hutu were killed in well-planned attacks ordered by the interim government, and Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines fuelled the killing. The RPF took the whole country by mid-July, and about two million Hutu fled, above all to Zaïre.

The RPF's army became the Rwandan Defence Force (RDF), replacing the old Forces Armées Rwandaises; enlistment is voluntary from 18. The RDF was a key belligerent in the First and Second Congo Wars, and was accused by a 2010 UN report of crimes against humanity in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which Rwanda denies; Kinshasa accused it of backing the M23 rebellion in 2012 and again in 2025, breaking off relations on 25 January after the Goma offensive. Rwanda is also among the top three contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping, and since July 2021 has fought Islamist insurgents in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado, more than 6,300 strong by 2026.
sections.governance:
The republic of 1962 inherited the colonial hierarchy with Hutu in command. Since July 1994 Rwanda has been a de facto one-party state ruled by the RPF, with Paul Kagame, its former commander, president since 2000. The constitution adopted by referendum in 2003 mandates a multi-party system but, in Article 54, forbids parties based on race, ethnic group, tribe, clan, region, sex or religion; in practice opposition parties are banned, critics arrested or assassinated and elections manipulated. The president, elected every five years, commands the Rwandan Defence Force.

Parliament has two chambers; the Chamber of Deputies has 80 members, 53 elected by proportional representation, 24 seats reserved for women and three for youth and disabled members. The law rests on German and Belgian civil law and custom and the death penalty is abolished. To clear the genocide cases the traditional village courts, Gacaca, were revived from 2004 to 2012 beside the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. In January 2006 twelve provinces became five and 106 districts thirty. A constitutional ombudsman fights corruption and officials, the president included, must declare their wealth; Transparency International ranked Rwanda fifth-cleanest in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2014. A new flag and anthem in 2001 removed ethnic references, and the 2002 census was the first since 1933 not to sort Rwandans into Hutu, Tutsi and Twa.
sections.impact:
The genocide of 1994 made Rwanda a byword for the failure of the international order, and reshaped the Great Lakes: the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was created to try its organisers, and the flight of two million Hutu into Zaïre and the RPF army's pursuit helped set off the First and Second Congo Wars. Relations with the Democratic Republic of the Congo have been tense ever since, and with France, whose ties to the Habyarimana regime led to a break in relations from 2006 to 2010. The RPF turned the country from the French-speaking world toward its English-speaking neighbours, joining the East African Community in 2007 and the Commonwealth in 2009.

Rwanda now projects power well beyond its size as one of the three largest contributors to UN peacekeeping and as an intervener in its own right, in Mozambique since 2021. Its health recovery, was called by Partners In Health among the most dramatic the world had seen in fifty years, and Kigali is counted among Africa's cleanest cities. The 'Visit Rwanda' campaign of 2018 bought sponsorships with Arsenal, Paris Saint-Germain and Atlético Madrid; Kigali hosted the UCI Road World Championships in September 2025. Lions, destroyed after 1994 when the parks became camps, returned in 2015. Films such as Hotel Rwanda carried the genocide's memory abroad; at home the week after Genocide Memorial Day, 7 April, is one of mourning and 4 July is Liberation Day.
sections.decline:
Thirty years after the genocide Rwanda is a paradox: admired for order, growth and low corruption, it ranks among the lowest in the world for transparency and civil liberties. The RPF has governed without real challenge since 1994 and Kagame since 2000. Human Rights Watch documents arbitrary detention, intimidation, disappearances, politically motivated trials and the massacre of peacefully protesting civilians, and torture is reported at Kami military camp and Gikondo prison. The press is tightly restricted and self-censors. The latest survey still counts 30.5% of the people in multidimensional poverty, and the density that Gérard Prunier sees as a part cause of 1994 keeps rising.

Abroad the old wounds reopen. Relations with Uganda collapsed in 2019 and the border was closed; the Democratic Republic of the Congo broke off relations on 25 January 2025 over renewed support for M23 after the Goma offensive. Tourism, the leading earner, was hit by COVID-19 and by the Ebola outbreak of 2026 in neighbouring Uganda and the DRC. Yet the economy grew 9.4% in 2025 with 7.5% forecast for 2026, 'Made in Rwanda' pushes industry, mobile money reaches nearly everyone, and Rwanda remains what it was before colonial rule, a unified state of one language and one people, its future resting on whether growth and reconciliation can outlast the system of control that has delivered them.

summary: Rwanda, a Hutu-dominated republic from independence in 1962, descended through coups and civil war into the 1994 genocide of up to a million Tutsi and moderate Hutu. Rebuilt under the Rwandan Patriotic Front and Paul Kagame, it has grown fast, fights in Congo and Mozambique and keeps peace for the UN, but tolerates no opposition.
references: Gérard Prunier, The Rwanda Crisis: History of a Genocide (Columbia University Press, 1995)
Jan Vansina, Antecedents to Modern Rwanda: The Nyiginya Kingdom (University of Wisconsin Press, 2004)
Philip Gourevitch, We Wish to Inform You That Tomorrow We Will Be Killed with Our Families (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1998)

pointDescs.1962: Rwanda becomes independent on 1 July under Grégoire Kayibanda after the Hutu revolution of 1959 and the referendum of 1961 that abolished the monarchy; attacks by Tutsi exiles and reprisals against Tutsi civilians follow.
pointDescs.1973: Juvénal Habyarimana takes power in a military coup; discrimination against Tutsi continues but violence lessens and the economy improves.
pointDescs.1990: The Rwandan Patriotic Front invades from Uganda, opening the Rwandan Civil War; by 1992 Habyarimana is forced into a coalition and in 1993 into the Arusha Accords.
pointDescs.1994: Habyarimana's plane is shot down on 6 April and the genocide begins: 500,000 to 1,000,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu are killed in about 100 days before the RPF takes the country in July; two million Hutu flee to Zaïre.
pointDescs.2000: Paul Kagame becomes president; the economy, tourism and the Human Development Index begin to grow rapidly from the ruins.
pointDescs.2003: A new constitution is adopted by referendum, replacing the transitional one of 1994; Gacaca courts begin trying genocide suspects in 2004.
pointDescs.2010: Rwanda's economy and services rebound; a UN report accuses its army of crimes against humanity in the Congo, which Rwanda denies; two independent newspapers are suspended before the election.
pointDescs.2017: The share of tourism revenue given to park communities rises to 10%; growth continues and poverty keeps falling.
pointDescs.2021: Life expectancy reaches 65.4 years; the Rwandan Defence Force deploys to Mozambique's Cabo Delgado in July.
pointDescs.2025: GDP grows 9.4%; Kigali hosts the UCI Road World Championships; the DRC severs relations on 25 January over the M23 Goma offensive. Rwanda is at the height of its regional power and reach.
